profiles.name: Alan de Mause
profiles.lived: active (Mel Bay catalog spans late 1970s through 2000s)
profiles.biography: Alan de Mause is a Mel Bay Publications author of jazz, fingerstyle, and chord-melody method books. *Mel Bay's Complete Fingerstyle Jazz Guitar Book* (2001) is his comprehensive method for solo fingerstyle jazz guitar, sequenced from physical mechanics through harmonization interval progression to mature jazz performance language. His pedagogical signature is the conversion of a lead sheet (single-note melody + chord symbols) into a complete fingerstyle solo arrangement via a progressive harmonization hierarchy (bare → thirds → tenths → sixths → oom-pah bass) governed at every step by ear-first pragmatism. Biography placeholder; refine with maintainer review on next pass.

profiles.name: Barry Galbraith
profiles.biography: Barry Galbraith (1919-1983) was an American jazz guitarist whose long studio career in New York from the 1940s through the 1970s made him one of the most-recorded jazz guitarists of his generation. His published work includes the *Jazz Solo Guitar* anthology — 42 fully notated chord-melody arrangements that teach by demonstration rather than by prose. Galbraith's approach is widely cited as foundational to the New York chord-melody tradition. Biography placeholder; refine with maintainer review.

profiles.name: Barry Harris
profiles.biography: American bebop pianist and educator. The sixth-diminished system documented in the Jazz Workshop is the seminal bebop harmonic method, widely adapted by guitarists for chord-melody and substitution work. Note: piano-pedagogy source, translatable directly to guitar voicings.

works.title: Jazz Workshop

profiles.name: George Benson
profiles.biography: Jazz guitarist and vocalist whose recording career spans from the Jack McDuff trio (early 1960s) through the soul-jazz crossover era of Breezin' (1976) to the vocal-pop work that defined his commercial peak. Originally trained as a bebop single-line player, Benson's harmonic vocabulary draws on tertian chord construction, the modal-substitution catalog of the natural-major harmonic field, and the chromatic color scales (harmonic minor, melodic minor, harmonic major) layered over diatonic progressions. The seven-volume George Benson Method (Jupiter Musical Group, 2019, co-authored with Peter Farrell) is the canonical written distillation of his playing approach. Vol. 1 (Chord Construction & Beginning Harmony) is the foundation; Vols. 2-7 build on it through advanced harmony, technique, approach tones, melodic-minor world, the Giant Lines, and the blues.

profiles.name: Bert Ligon
profiles.biography: American jazz educator and author. Connecting Chords with Linear Harmony (1996) is a canonical text on linear voice-leading and chord-progression generation. Concert-pitch pedagogy translatable to guitar.

profiles.instrument: 6-string guitar; theory framework applies to all instruments
profiles.biography: Brent Vaartstra is a contemporary American jazz guitarist, educator, and the founder of Learn Jazz Standards (LearnJazzStandards.com) and the Learn Jazz Standards podcast. *The Jazz Standards Playbook* (2019) is his ten-standards method for self-taught jazz improvisation, centered on an ear-first acquisition protocol he calls LIST (Listen / Internalize / Sing / Transfer) and a relational, function-driven approach to harmonic analysis. profiles.name: Dirk Laukens
profiles.biography: Dirk Laukens is a Belgian jazz guitarist and educator who founded JazzGuitar.be — one of the most widely-used online jazz-guitar pedagogy resources, with a catalog of PDF method books, lessons, and free-tier instructional articles. His method materials are characterized by systematic shape-based pedagogy (moveable chord and scale shapes), function-assigned vocabulary, and substitution-derivation taxonomies organized around concrete jazz standards. profiles.name: Gene Bertoncini
profiles.biography: Gene Bertoncini (1937-) is an American jazz guitarist whose nylon-string chord-melody approach — heard on his long discography and in particular the duo recordings with bassist Michael Moore — is widely cited as foundational to the New York chord-melody tradition. *Arrangements for Solo Guitar*, transcribed by Jason Ennis and Chris Ullrich from his *Body and Soul* and *Quiet Now* CDs, documents 24 of his solo arrangements alongside a glossary of his characteristic open-string voicings. The book teaches by demonstration; its only prose appears in the Preface and the Transcribers' Notes. Biography placeholder; refine with maintainer review.

profiles.name: Greg O'Rourke
profiles.biography: Greg O'Rourke is a jazz guitar educator behind JazzGuitar.Be, an online jazz guitar pedagogy platform. *Complete Chord Melody* codifies a procedural teach-yourself method for solo chord-melody arrangement, organized around a four-step recipe and a painting-by-numbers voicing-lookup system. Status is pedagogue (P-bucket per #345): real teaching influence, not a master voice. Biography placeholder; refine with maintainer review on next pass.

profiles.name: George Heussenstamm & Roni Silbergleit
profiles.biography: George Heussenstamm and Roni Silbergleit are the joint authors of *Goldmine: 100 Jazz Lessons* (2005), a comprehensive jazz guitar method organized around the ii-V-I progression as the irreducible harmonic cell from which all jazz vocabulary radiates. The book's pedagogical signature is the one-way progression gate: each layer is introduced as a stepping stone toward its own transcendence. Biography placeholder; refine with maintainer review.

profiles.name: Howard Roberts
profiles.biography: American studio guitarist and educator, Wrecking Crew session veteran. Known for terse pragmatic teaching emphasizing chord-melody arrangements and bebop vocabulary. Author of Chord Melody and Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks.

profiles.name: Jamey Aebersold
profiles.instrument: saxophone (primary); pedagogical method applies to all instruments
profiles.biography: Jamey Aebersold (1939-) is an American jazz educator whose Jamey Aebersold Jazz catalog of play-along volumes (Vol. 1 *How To Play Jazz and Improvise* through 130+ subsequent volumes) is the most widely-used jazz-improvisation practice method in American music education. His pioneering insight — that a recorded rhythm section can supply tempo, harmony, and feel for self-directed practice — turned jazz improvisation from an apprentice-only skill into a self-teachable curriculum. profiles.name: Jens Larsen
profiles.biography: Jens Larsen is a Danish jazz guitarist and educator active in the modern jazz pedagogical tradition. Through book-length works in the Fundamental Changes series and an extensive online presence, his teaching codifies a structured vocabulary of arpeggio substitutions, chromatic enclosures, and altered/diminished scale applications, organized around shared-tone analysis and voice-leading discipline. profiles.name: Jerry Bergonzi
profiles.instrument: tenor saxophone (primary); pedagogical works widely applied across instruments including guitar
profiles.biography: Jerry Bergonzi is an American jazz tenor saxophonist and educator whose *Inside Improvisation* series (Advance Music) is a foundational pedagogical corpus on melodic, harmonic, and rhythmic improvisation. Vol. 4 (Melodic Rhythms) treats rhythm as an independent compositional domain — included in batch-1 as a non-guitar source whose rhythmic systems transfer directly to guitar improvisation (line construction, comping, ensemble interaction). profiles.name: Jerry Coker
profiles.instrument: saxophone (primary); pedagogical materials applicable to all instruments
profiles.biography: Jerry Coker (1932-2018) was an American saxophonist, composer, and one of the most influential jazz educators of the 20th century. As a long-time professor at the University of Tennessee and author of foundational jazz-pedagogy texts — *Patterns for Jazz* (1970, with Casale, Campbell, Greene), *Improvising Jazz* (1964), and *Elements of the Jazz Language for the Developing Improvisor* (1991) — Coker codified the American jazz-pedagogy tradition into a teachable, transferable curriculum. His thesis that jazz improvisation is a finite learnable language constructed from a small set of named devices is now widely accepted as the operating epistemology of contemporary jazz education. profiles.name: Jim Hall
profiles.biography: Influential jazz comper and soloist (1930-2013) whose voicings emphasize space, fourths, and conversational interaction. Studied composition and arrangement formally; recordings with Bill Evans, Sonny Rollins, Paul Desmond, and Art Farmer defined a quieter, more dialogic approach to jazz guitar accompaniment. Authored Exploring Jazz Guitar (Hal Leonard) and Jazz Guitar Environments (1994).

profiles.name: Jimmy Bruno
profiles.biography: Philadelphia-born jazz guitarist trained in the bebop tradition; sideman with Buddy Rich and Lionel Hampton in the 1970s before establishing his own quartet and a long pedagogical career. Bruno's published method centers on right-hand technique as a habit-formation problem: a three-rule directional picking system (down to higher string, up to lower, alternate on same string), justified by economy of motion, replaces strict alternate picking as the basis for jazz line playing. The Art of Picking (2002) is the canonical written distillation of this approach; companion volumes (notably Six Essential Fingerings for the Jazz Guitarist) supply the scale/fingering substrate the picking method is applied to.

works.title: The Art of Picking

profiles.name: Jody Fisher
profiles.biography: Educator (1957-) whose Alfred Music series — Complete Jazz Guitar Method (Beginning / Intermediate / Mastering), Jazz Guitar Harmony, Chord Tone Soloing — systematized jazz guitar study for generations of self-taught players. Fisher's contribution is pedagogical structure rather than distinctive personal style: he codified the standard voicing vocabulary (drop-2, drop-3, extended harmonies, altered chords) into an ordered curriculum and provided 'hundreds of chord voicings and improvisation ideas' across the series.

profiles.name: Joe Pass
profiles.biography: Bebop guitarist whose solo recordings (Virtuoso series, 1973-1983) reset expectations for unaccompanied jazz guitar. Combined walking bass lines with chord stabs and single-note runs from held chord positions.

profiles.name: Johnny Smith
profiles.biography: Master of close-voiced chord-melody (1922-2013). His 1952 'Moonlight in Vermont' (Royal Roost) became a template for the genre — tight closed voicings that 'are a finger stretch on guitar' and 'pianistic' in feel. Authored the Johnny Smith Approach to Guitar (Mel Bay). His playing combines closed-position chord voicings with 'rapidly ascending lines... more diatonic than chromatically-based' (Django-like but diatonic).

Chord Solos

profiles.name: Lenny Breau
profiles.biography: Canadian guitarist (1941-1984) who synthesized jazz, country, flamenco, folk, and classical idioms. Renowned for right-hand finger independence — bass, chord, and melody as three simultaneously moving voices — and for taking Chet Atkins's harp-harmonic technique to unprecedented levels. Later in his career played a custom 7-string with a high A tuned two octaves above the 5th string. Cited as a primary influence by Bill Frisell, Pat Metheny, and many others.

profiles.name: Martin Taylor
profiles.biography: Scottish virtuoso whose solo fingerstyle approach extends the Django Reinhardt and Joe Pass traditions with greater fluidity in thumb-bass / chord / melody independence. Played a decade with Stéphane Grappelli; authored Solo Jazz Guitar (Mel Bay), Single Note Soloing (Mel Bay), the Fingerstyle Jazz Guitar DVD with Grossman's Guitar Workshop, and runs the Martin Taylor Guitar Academy with extensive online lessons. Cites Bill Evans and Art Tatum as keyboard influences for melody-bass separation.

profiles.name: Matt Warnock
profiles.instrument: 6-string electric guitar; pedagogical materials applicable to acoustic
profiles.biography: Matt Warnock is a contemporary jazz guitarist and online educator whose MattWarnockGuitar.com publishes a long catalog of beginner-to-intermediate jazz-guitar method materials. His *Beginner's Guide to Jazz Guitar* (compact PDF + accompanying video) is the entry-level title in that catalog, organized around a single ii V I progression in C major as the unifying harmonic vehicle. Warnock's pedagogical signature is the named-rule-governed-technique form: every technique is given a precise structural definition, an acquisition sequence, and a self-extension protocol via variation. profiles.biography: American jazz guitarist and Berklee educator. The Advancing Guitarist (1987) and the Almanac of Guitar Voice Leading (4 vols) are the canonical voice-leading texts in jazz guitar pedagogy.

profiles.name: Mickey Baker
profiles.biography: Kentucky-born guitarist whose recording career bridged the 1950s R&B/early-rock-and-roll session world (Mickey & Sylvia's "Love Is Strange", Atlantic and Savoy sessions for Ray Charles, Big Joe Turner, Ruth Brown, LaVern Baker) and the Paris-based jazz expat community where he lived from the 1960s onward. The Complete Course in Jazz Guitar (Lewis Music Publishing Co., 1955) — universally known as Mickey Baker's Vol. 1 — is among the most-cited and most-used jazz-guitar method books ever written; its 26 lessons introduce the working-musician's chord vocabulary (the "Baker chords"), substitution lattice, comping and rhythm patterns, and single-note line vocabulary as a unified practical system rather than a theoretical exposition. A Volume 2 followed.

profiles.name: Nelson Faria
profiles.instrument: 6-string nylon-string guitar (primary); 7-string and electric also documented in catalog
profiles.biography: Nelson Faria is a Brazilian jazz guitarist, composer, and educator whose *The Brazilian Guitar Book* (1995, Sher Music Co.) is the canonical English-language performance methodology for Brazilian guitar styles. His pedagogical approach centers body-first internalization (clap-and-foot drills) and a strict thumb-finger texture split that codifies five regional rhythmic vocabularies (Samba, Bossa Nova, Choro, Frevo, Baião) as deployable repertoires switched at structural moments. profiles.name: Nicolas Slonimsky
profiles.biography: Russian-American composer, conductor, lexicographer, and music theorist. Best known to jazz musicians for the Thesaurus of Scales and Melodic Patterns (1947), a systematic enumeration of melodic possibility space via equal divisions of the octave plus polation operations (infrapolation, interpolation, ultrapolation). The Thesaurus became foundational source material for John Coltrane (whose Giant Steps cycle is the equal-division-of-octave-by-three pattern from this book), Pat Martino, and many post-bop and modern jazz innovators. Slonimsky himself was not a jazz player; his contribution is taxonomic — the catalog of every melodic move that fits any given scale context.

profiles.name: Pat Martino
profiles.instrument: 6-string electric guitar (primary); steel-string, semi-hollow archtop most associated with his sound
profiles.biography: Pat Martino (1944-2021) was an American jazz guitarist and composer whose 1989 method *Linear Expressions* (Hal Leonard) codifies his lifelong harmonic-structure-first approach to improvisation. Martino's work centers the conviction that harmonic structure dictates melodic choice — that every line form on the neck is determined by the chord inversion the player is voicing under it, not by free melodic invention. His system reduces the full complexity of jazz harmony to five 'activity' forms drawn from the relative-minor relationship plus a small set of interval-formula substitutions that handle every altered or complex chord. Biography placeholder; refine with maintainer review on next pass.

profiles.name: Peter Bernstein
profiles.biography: Brooklyn-born jazz guitarist whose playing and teaching extend the post-bop lineage of Wes Montgomery, Grant Green, and Jim Hall. Sideman recordings with Lou Donaldson, Sonny Rollins, Diana Krall, and Larry Goldings situate his aesthetic in a melody-primary, narrative-driven approach to improvisation that treats jazz as a language rather than a vocabulary of scales. Bernstein teaches privately and at NYU; the 2023 master's thesis by Nico Moreno (also at NYU) is the canonical written distillation of his teaching, transcribed from Bernstein-consented lesson recordings. The masters.json entry is sourced from the Moreno thesis, not from a Bernstein-authored method.

profiles.name: Randy Felts
profiles.biography: Randy Felts is a long-time Berklee College of Music faculty member whose 2002 *Reharmonization Techniques* (Berklee Press) is the canonical English-language reference for systematic jazz and contemporary chord-substitution craft. The book's characteristic stance is restraint — substitution is presented as a precision tool governed by explicit stop-rules and application limits, not as wholesale chord-replacement. profiles.name: Ted Dunbar
profiles.instrument: 6-string electric guitar; theory/composition framework applies to all instruments
profiles.biography: Ted Dunbar (1937-1998) was an American jazz guitarist, composer, and influential educator who taught at Rutgers University. Acknowledged in his own published works, his circle of mentors and collaborators included David Baker and George Russell — and his theoretical work sits alongside Russell's Lydian Chromatic Concept as a foundational American jazz-theory tradition. *A System of Tonal Convergence* (1975, self-published) codifies his harmonic framework: the tonal gravity law as a single founding axiom from which a complete improvisational and compositional method extends. Dunbar's characteristic move is to treat the entire chromatic scale as always available, governed by five awareness factors rather than fixed prescriptive rules. profiles.name: Ted Greene
profiles.biography: Los Angeles teacher and player whose lessons and the openly-distributed tedgreene.com archive reshaped how guitarists think about four-note voicings, voice-leading, and the relationship between melody and harmony. Authored Chord Chemistry (1971) and Modern Chord Progressions (1973). His V-System — a taxonomy of 14 voicing groups across 43 unique four-note chord qualities — is the canonical Greene framework.

profiles.name: Wes Montgomery
profiles.biography: Self-taught Indianapolis guitarist whose innovations after 1959 reshaped jazz guitar: thumb-attack right hand, parallel-octave melodic statements, and block-chord chorus climaxes built directly from melodic shape. Active recording career 1959-1968 (Riverside, Verve, A&M) with canonical statements on Smokin' at the Half Note (1965) and The Incredible Jazz Guitar of Wes Montgomery (1960). No instructional book of his own; documentation is via transcription collections and biographical studies.
